item.title: What Happens in the Brain When Cannabis Is Used Every Day
item.description:
Cannabis

What Happens in the Brain When Cannabis Is Used Every Day

Why regular cannabis use is fundamentally different from occasional use.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Daily cannabis use is very different from occasional use.
  • Repeated THC exposure may gradually shift the brain into a different operating state.
  • Feeling "normal" after cannabis may mean return to an adapted brain state, not the brain's original baseline.
  • The brain learns what it repeats. The same neuroplasticity underlying addiction also makes recovery possible.

I've heard countless times that "Cannabis doesn't really get me high anymore. I just use it to feel normal." For years, I thought the answer was straightforward: tolerance to the drug. That's also true—but it is an incomplete answer.

A fascinating new study by Katharina Lege and colleagues at Maastricht University will be published on July 15th. It suggests something else may be happening. Tolerance does not mean the brain has recovered. It means the brain has adapted to cannabis.

Rather than examining individual brain regions, the investigators studied how THC changes the brain's dynamic brain states—the constantly shifting patterns of communication among large-scale brain networks. They found not only acute changes after THC exposure, but also persistent neuroadaptations in chronic users. Together, these findings raise an intriguing possibility: repeated cannabis use may gradually produce an adapted new normal operating brain state. This adaptive "Brain on THC" is not simply repeated episodes of intoxication.

The Brain Is Always Changing

Lege's new study examined how THC affects these dynamic brain states in both occasional and chronic cannabis users. Using a double-blind, placebo-controlled design, they found that THC use reduced the brain's ability to enter one highly integrated state associated with efficient communication across multiple brain networks. Participants also performed worse on tests of sustained attention, particularly occasional users.

These findings fit decades of research showing that acute cannabis impairs attention, working memory, executive function, psychomotor performance, and judgment, even when users appear outwardly functional.

But the more novel and important finding involved chronic users. Although daily users reported feeling less intoxicated after THC—a familiar sign of tolerance—the investigators also found their brains already differed before receiving the drug. Chronic users were not simply less intoxicated; their brains had already undergone measurable neuroadaptation to daily use of the drug.

Tolerance Means Adaptation

Lege also reported that both the immediate effects of THC and the persistent changes seen in chronic users closely tracked the brain's own natural cannabinoid receptor(CB1) distribution, through which THC acts. Chronic THC causes the brain's endocannabinoid system to adapt, reducing endogenous CB1 receptor availability, with gradual recovery after abstinence. Withdrawal symptoms—including irritability, anxiety, insomnia, reduced appetite, and craving—provide additional evidence that the brain has produced a "new normal" in response to repeated THC exposure.

article continues after advertisement

Traditionally, cannabis intoxication has been viewed as an episodic event: use cannabis, become intoxicated, then return to baseline. The newer neuroscience suggests another possibility for daily cannabis users: the brain's normal baseline has been altered. The question becomes, "What happens when someone gets high?" but also, "What happens when the brain adapts to being high every day?"

A Different Way to Think About Daily Cannabis Use

Rather than producing isolated effects on individual receptors or circuits, repeated THC exposure appears to induce coordinated neuroplastic changes across multiple interacting brain systems to produce an adapted-to-THC brain operating state. Continued cannabis use temporarily maintains that state, while abstinence unmasks the neurobiological adaptations that developed during chronic exposure.

Why do so many daily cannabis users say they no longer use cannabis to become intoxicated but simply to feel "normal?" They are maintaining the neuroadapted state their brain has gradually learned to expect. They are not restoring their original brain function.

Feeling normal is not necessarily the same as functioning as you did before regular cannabis use. Daily users may feel normal because their brains have recalibrated their internal baselines. Recovery, then, is not simply eliminating THC—it is allowing the brain to establish a new, drug-free equilibrium through recovery-related neuroplasticity.

The Brain Learns What it Repeats

One of the brain's greatest strengths is its remarkable ability to learn from repeated experience-practice makes neural circuits more efficient. Practice strengthens the neural circuits that are used most often. The same principle applies to repeated cannabis use. Each episode of THC exposure reinforces neural pathways that link cannabis with relief, reward, or routine. Over months or years of daily use, cannabis may gradually become the brain's default response to stress, boredom, anxiety, sleeplessness, or emotional discomfort. What begins as a conscious choice becomes an increasingly automatic learned response.

From the brain's perspective, this is simply efficient learning. Eventually, the adapted brain comes to expect THC as part of its normal operating environment. Feeling "normal" without cannabis may then require another round of neuroplasticity as the brain relearns how to regulate mood, sleep, motivation, and reward on its own.

article continues after advertisement

Repeated cannabis use also teaches the brain associations that may not be adaptive. If THC is repeatedly paired with falling asleep, managing stress, socializing, or having sex, those normal activities may gradually become linked to the drug itself. Over time, the brain may begin to expect THC before these experiences feel natural or rewarding. What began as a learned association eventually becomes an expectation, reinforcing continued cannabis use.

A New Framework

The Lege study does not demonstrate that daily cannabis use creates a distinct brain state. It does show that THC perturbs dynamic brain states, that chronic users exhibit persistent neuroadaptations even before receiving THC, and that both the acute and persistent changes observed with daily use closely follow the brain's CB1 receptor distribution. Together with decades of research on tolerance, withdrawal, and CB1 receptor regulation, these findings support an intriguing—but still unproven—clinical hypothesis: repeated THC exposure gradually shifts the brain toward an adapted cannabis operating state, one that differs fundamentally from the transient effects experienced by occasional users.

Evolution designed the brain to adapt because adaptation usually improves survival. The brain is not malfunctioning when it adapts to repeated THC exposure. It is doing exactly what healthy brains evolved to do—modify their function in response to repeated experience. The problem is that this remarkable capacity for adaptation becomes organized around a powerful pharmacologic reward rather than the natural rewards that normally shape motivation, learning, decision-making, and behavior.

This chronic cannabis framework is conceptually similar to the one I have used to understand opioid use disorder (OUD). In both conditions, repeated drug exposure stimulates endogenous receptor systems and elicits compensatory neuroadaptations that help maintain function in the continued presence of the drug. Those adaptations ultimately shift the brain toward a new operating state.

article continues after advertisement

Repeated drug use temporarily maintains that tenuous adapted state, whereas abstinence reveals—quite dramatically in OUD—the underlying neurobiological changes. The important differences lie in the magnitude, clinical manifestations, and risks of the two disorders—not necessarily in the fundamental principle of neuroadaptation.

If this emerging framework continues to be supported, addiction may be understood as if it were repeated single intoxications, but as chronic neuroadaptation. That shift is necessary to change how we think about prevention, preaddiction, treatment, and recovery by focusing greater attention on preserving or restoring healthy brain function through recovery-related neuroplasticity rather than simply eliminating the drug.

The next question is equally important. If the brain can learn to depend on THC, how does it relearn to function without it? That question—and the science of recovery-related neuroplasticity—is the subject of the next article in this series.

item.title: What Misspelled Words Reveal About Connection
item.description:
Psychology

What Misspelled Words Reveal About Connection

Personal Perspective: Tiny errors can show personality, closeness, and context.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Misspellings are judged through context, not just correctness.
  • A small typo can make a message feel warmer and more human.
  • People often read mistakes more generously when trust already exists.
  • Correcting errors is most helpful when it protects someone from later embarrassment.
Written communication often asks us to present a polished version of ourselves.
Source: Jakub Zerdzicki / Pexels

Some misspelled words make us pause. Others make us smile.

A typo in a formal report may irritate. A misspelled name may feel careless. A repeated error in an important document may raise questions about attention to detail. But in everyday life, misspelled words are not always read as failures.

Sometimes they become oddly charming.

They show movement, mood, personality and the small human messiness inside communication.

Why Some Mistakes Feel Endearing

Think of “mabey” instead of “maybe.”

The meaning is clear. Nobody is confused. Yet the word carries something extra. It feels quick, unedited and slightly playful, as if the thought arrived faster than the fingers could organise it.

It is wrong, technically. But emotionally, it may feel warm.

That is the psychology of misspelled words. They are not only linguistic errors. They are social signals.

Written communication often asks us to present a polished version of ourselves. We proofread emails, tidy messages and correct spelling because writing is easily judged. In professional settings, clean language can signal competence, care and credibility.

That is why a small typo in a job application or important email can feel more embarrassing than it deserves to be.

But not all writing is a performance of professionalism. Much of it is relational. We text friends, message partners, respond to colleagues, leave notes for children, send quick jokes and unfinished ideas.

In those spaces, misspellings can soften communication rather than damage it. They can make the person behind the words feel more present.

The Brain Reads For Intention

When someone writes “definately,” “tommorow,” “becuase” or “mabey,” we usually know what they meant.

The mind repairs the word almost instantly. But during that tiny moment of repair, we also register something about the person. They may have been moving quickly, thinking aloud, distracted, excited, tired or relaxed.

A misspelling can therefore become a trace of real life.

It says: this message was made by a person, not a machine. It was sent in the middle of a day. It came from someone doing several things at once, or from someone who trusted the relationship enough not to polish every edge.

That is why a small mistake in a friendly message can feel more intimate than a flawless sentence. It lets the unedited self appear.

Imperfection Can Create Warmth

Small imperfections can make people feel more approachable.

When someone seems too polished, they may impress us, but they can also feel distant. A tiny mistake lowers that distance. It reminds us that the other person is competent but human, thoughtful but not perfectly controlled.

This is why misspellings are judged so differently depending on who makes them.

If a stranger sends a careless message full of errors, we may see the mistakes as signs of low effort. If a close friend sends the same message, we may barely notice, or find it funny.

If a child writes “becos” instead of “because,” it may feel precious. If a partner repeatedly misspells a word in the same way, it can become part of the private language of the relationship.

Over time, these quirks can become affectionate markers. Families develop shared spellings. Friends repeat old typos as jokes. Couples keep strange little phrases alive for years.

A word that began as a mistake becomes a memory. It belongs to the relationship.

When Correction Helps

Of course, some misspellings matter.

Names matter. Public documents matter. Medical, legal and financial communication require precision. In those settings, correcting an error is not pedantic. It is protective. Accuracy can be a form of care.

But in lower-stakes communication, correction is more complicated.

To correct someone is not simply to fix a word. It changes the emotional tone of the exchange. It can say, “I want to help you.” It can also say, “I noticed your mistake.”

And in the wrong setting, it can feel like a tiny public ranking: I am the one who knows; you are the one who got it wrong.

A better question than “Is this word misspelled?” is: “Does correcting it help?”

If the mistake could embarrass the person later, correct it gently and privately. If the meaning is clear and the exchange is casual, perhaps let it go.

Sometimes the misspelled word is not getting in the way of communication. Sometimes it is part of the communication.

What Typos Reveal About Us

Misspelled words also reveal how much generosity we bring to interpretation.

The same error can annoy us or endear us depending on our mood, relationship and assumptions. When we like someone, we often read their mistakes kindly. When we are frustrated with them, even a typo can become evidence.

The word itself has not changed. Our interpretation has.

That makes misspellings a useful mirror. They show us not only how others communicate, but how we judge.

Do we read small mistakes as signs of stupidity, laziness, or lack of care? Or do we allow for speed, context, emotion, and humanity?

The generous reading is not always naive. It is often more accurate. People are rarely reducible to their typos. A misspelled word may simply mean that someone was tired, hurried, laughing, distracted or comfortable enough to be informal.

So when a misspelled word appears, pause before correcting it.

There are times to fix the word. There are times to ignore it. And there are times to enjoy it.

Sometimes the mistake is not the opposite of connection. Sometimes it is the evidence of it.

A misspelled word can be a tiny reminder that language is alive. It bends, slips, stumbles and still finds its way — not because it is wrong, but because it feels real.

item.title: Finding More Humor, Hope, and Joy in Everyday Life
item.description:
Laughter

Finding More Humor, Hope, and Joy in Everyday Life

How small moments of laughter help us carry the hard parts better.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Hope helps us move forward, even when life feels uncertain or heavy.
  • Making room for humour helps lighten the load without minimizing the hard.
  • Looking for the funny, the hope-filled, and the joyful changes how we experience our days.

A key cornerstone of wellness is knowing how to have fun and find moments of lightness. The art of cultivating laughter, pleasure, and play, and knowing how to enjoy moments of merriment, is what resilient people do.

Yet when life feels heavy, humour is often one of the first things to disappear. Hope can feel out of reach. Ironically, these are often the moments we need both the most. As I share in I Hope So, “Hope keeps us moving forward, with a view to a brighter horizon even when the road is hard, while humour lightens the journey, offering moments of levity that remind us of our humanity” (Hanley-Dafoe, 2026, p. 115).

Hope helps us believe tomorrow can be different. Humour helps us make it through today. Together, they remind us that even difficult seasons can hold moments of lightness and that while life is hard, there is still room for tenderness, connection, playfulness, and joy.

Why Humour Matters

Humour reminds us not to take ourselves too seriously while still holding space for compassion, fun, light-heartedness, and tenderness despite the stressors, hurt, and pain we all experience. It affords us brief moments of relief and reprieve and helps lift the weight off our shoulders.

Research continues to demonstrate that laughter decreases stress hormones like cortisol, releases endorphins, soothes away built-up tension, and provides temporary pain relief. Over time, regular laughter has even been associated with improved immune function.

Just as importantly, humour changes our perspective. It creates space between us and our stress. Mental health and well-being expert and comedian Jessica Holmes talks about how seeing our stories and experiences through a comedic lens can help create enough distance that we start to see things differently (Life by Design, 2026). Instead of feeling completely buried beneath our circumstances, we begin to experience our stressors as something we are navigating rather than something we are consumed by.

Practical Strategies to Cultivate Joy, Humour, and Hope

Lightheartedness allows space for the belief that “all will be well” to take root. Like any aspect of resilience, humour, hope, and joy can be intentionally cultivated through small, everyday practices.

  1. Set the intention to look for it: Our brains naturally notice what we repeatedly search for. When we intentionally look for moments of joy, kindness, beauty, hope, or humour, we begin to find more of them. Start a note in your phone where you capture funny moments from your day. Notice acts of kindness. Collect and keep track of signs of hope. The looking is the practice.
  2. Borrow a different perspective: Ask your children, partner, or loved ones, “When am I at my best with you?” or “What is your favourite thing that I do with you?” You might be surprised by what’s most meaningful. Another practice Jessica shared with me is imagining a particularly difficult week as though it were an episode of a sitcom. The situation itself may not have changed, but our relationship to it often does. That little bit of distance creates room for perspective, creativity, and possibility.
  3. Use playful pattern interrupts: Ask an unexpected question at the dinner table, in a meeting, or during a stressful day. “What's your third favourite animal?” “What's one thing that made you smile today?” Sometimes a simple shift in attention is enough to reset the emotional tone of a conversation.
  4. Choose laughter on purpose: Seek out things that reliably make you smile and laugh. Watch a comedy instead of another heavy drama or crime documentary. Read a funny book. Listen to comedians. Tell the funny, exaggerated story. Watch silly videos. Share memes with friends. Research even suggests that anticipating laughter boosts dopamine before the event itself (Berk et al., 2008). Planning something enjoyable gives your brain something hopeful to anticipate.
  5. Create your own joy playbook: We often assume we'll remember what restores us. In difficult seasons, we usually don't. Create a list of the people, places, activities, traditions, and experiences that reliably bring you joy. What makes you laugh every time? What leaves you feeling energized rather than depleted? What makes time seem to disappear? Who fills your cup? Write them down and return to your list when you need a lift.
  6. Lean on your signature strengths: Jessica wears a bracelet with two of her signature strengths, humour and kindness, and looks at it before she walks into a new situation or a room. It is a small, physical reminder of what she wants to lead with. What would it look like to name your own strengths and let them set the tone before you walk into a hard conversation, a new room, or a busy week?
  7. Reconnect with your favourite self: Think about a time when you felt most like yourself. Perhaps you were laughing easily, feeling curious, playful, calm, or deeply connected with the people around you. What were you doing? Who were you with? What qualities were you embodying?
article continues after advertisement

The Importance of Sitting With What’s Hard

None of this is about forcing positivity or minimizing the hard. I do not believe everything happens for a reason or that every hardship comes with a silver lining. Some things just suck.

Sometimes the most loving thing we can do is simply acknowledge that something is difficult. We do not have to rush someone toward gratitude. We do not need to solve every problem. Sometimes sitting beside someone and saying, "This is hard," is enough.

One of my favourite questions to ask is: “Is there anything I can do that wouldn't make this worse?” Holding space for someone's pain is one of the greatest gifts we can offer.

Final Thoughts

The same season that stretches us can also surprise us with moments of kindness, beauty, and unexpected laughter. Stay curious enough to notice the funny, open enough to receive the joy, and hopeful enough to believe another good moment is still coming.

This week, ask yourself:

What brought a smile to my face?

Who helped me laugh?

What gave me hope?

What made today feel a little lighter?

Sometimes resilience isn't built through one extraordinary breakthrough. More often, it grows through the ordinary practice of noticing that even while carrying the hard, there is still goodness to be found. Every hope-filled moment, every shared laugh, every act of kindness, and every glimpse of joy becomes evidence that the hard is never the whole story. And when we share those moments with others, we help them notice what they may have overlooked and remind one another that we were never meant to carry life's challenges alone.

item.title: Your Social Self-Portrait
item.description:
Social Networking

Your Social Self-Portrait

How can we map our social networks to learn more about ourselves?

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • One measure of who we are is the people we relate to.
  • It is hard to count or draw our social networks.
  • New software has been designed to help us create our social self-portraits
  • The process of creating your social self-portrait will show who has helped make you who you are.

We’ve come a long way from the 17th century, when you had to be Rembrandt to own a self-portrait. Now we have a lot of ways of representing who we are: selfies, CV’s, social media sites, family trees, and memoirs. Some people write their own obituaries. But we’re still missing a way of capturing the thing that most distinguishes each of us: our social networks. One measure of who we are is the people we relate to.

My recent 75th birthday got me wondering: If it takes a village to raise a child, what does it take to raise a 75-year-old? A city, maybe—at least a much larger number of people along the way, people who shape our lives. Though it’s more precious to me than my money or my possessions, both of which are relatively easy to count and value, my social network is hard to number or draw.

How could I make a picture of these relationships, or a sculpture? I tried starting a list of the people who currently play an important role in my life and quickly faced one of the reasons we don’t make our social self-portraits: it’s complicated.

If you’ve ever tried to list just your relatives in Ancestry.com, you know what I mean. You can spend many hours trying to fill in the boxes of your blood relatives over several generations. And yet, only some of those people matter to you currently. You could try your Facebook or LinkedIn lists, but that would only capture a small and self-selected slice of those who matter to you.

I soon realized that I’m an old guy with a problem that only a younger tech mind can help me with. But none of the younger, tech-wiser people I asked about this problem knew of a popular way to create a social self-portrait. So, assuming there has to be software for every good idea, I spent some time searching the web for software that could help: “social self-portrait,” “social networks software,” “graphic design for social self-portraits.” Nothing came close to what I have in mind.

Then I asked Google’s AI mode: “What software can help me create my social network self-portrait?” In a flash, it understood my question and gave me five suggestions: Kumu, Gephi, SocNetV, Creately, and Flourish. Kumu seems the most promising for my needs. (The others are too technical or for social scientists.)

The social self-portrait could develop into a fascinating new art form, possible now because of graphic design options that can manage big data. Mapping social networks is like mapping a matrix of molecules or the stars in a galaxy. Your bridge club might look like a benzene ring; your Facebook followers might look like the Milky Way.

I picture my people in clusters of different sizes and shapes, at various distances from me and from each other. It’s hard to imagine how I might arrange them in space, and harder still to imagine how this self-portrait changes over time.

Kumu organizes its social maps by “elements” (people or organizations), “connections” (the type of relationship), and “loops” (the interconnections among people or organizations, or clusters). Building these maps begins with a database. I’m going to try to start with the contacts in my phone or our Christmas card list Excel spreadsheet. Then I’ll have to weed out the people who don’t fit and add data I need, like the cluster(s) they belong to.

article continues after advertisement

Can this old dog learn this new trick? Kumu promises I can, and they will help me.

Why should I bother? Why should you? For the same reason that we bother to take selfies, draw our faces, gaze in the mirror, write diaries and memoirs. We have always been fascinated by ourselves, and always will be. Now we have a chance to create another kind of self-portrait, one that represents the people who have made us who we are. Who cares how long it takes? Every time you add someone, you’re counting your blessings.

item.title: How to Develop Your Personal Leadership Potential
item.description:
Leadership

How to Develop Your Personal Leadership Potential

Research clearly provides a roadmap for effective leadership development.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Leadership development is hard; it takes time and daily devotion.
  • If leaders focus on followers and their development in helping to lead, they will be more effective.

A while back, I was interviewed about how to better develop one’s leadership capacity and potential. Here are my answers, which include some clear lessons learned from research and practice on leadership development.

1. What does it take to develop your leadership capacity?

First and foremost, developing as a leader is hard work. You need motivation and commitment, and you need to work on it daily (Day, 2024). Moreover, you need to move beyond self-focus. Most leadership development programs should be better termed “leader development.” “Leadership development” focuses on what leaders and followers do together: co-creating leadership. Therefore, to be effective, leaders need to be able to build leadership capacity in followers—in teams. The very best leaders succeed because they engage their followers in the process, and together, leaders and followers create leadership.

You need a plan. There are several models in the book, and some may resonate more with a particular individual. Work at it every day. Get feedback. We’re big on assessments. Also, it’s important to evaluate your progress.

2. As a result of COVID and the major shift to the virtual workplace, what are your thoughts on similarities and differences for leadership development in the virtual and hybrid environment?

I don’t think things have changed all that much—many leaders already are doing some of their leadership virtually, with distributed teams, global organizations, and geographic distribution, etc. [Zoom meetings for research teams]. The change is that leaders now have to do much or all of the leading virtually. But it’s all about communication, and realizing the strengths and limitations of various communication modalities…

I think that virtual work is going to be more common going forward because it worked better than many had expected.

3. You have been writing books on leadership for many years. What is your favorite leadership topic and why?

I’ve written for a long time on charismatic and transformational leadership, so that’s still a favorite. Transformational leadership is “charisma plus”—leaders who are inspirational and positive role models, but they are also able to connect with followers, establish good working relationships with them, empower them, and together lead. Transformational leaders also push their followers to be creative and innovative. It’s a good model to follow for leader development (and it’s in the book in detail).

I’m also interested in “good/ethical” and “bad” leadership. There are some interesting findings there. For example, when you ask people to name the qualities/characteristics they want in a leader, the majority will mention positive characteristics (honesty or integrity, empathetic and responsive, supportive, etc.), but a subset will mention what we might call “anti-prototypical” qualities (manipulative, pushy, self-centered, aggressive). What that means is that while most of us want positive and other-oriented qualities in our leaders, some of us want the “strong, tough individual who will fight.” There are a lot of interesting dichotomies like that when it comes to leadership.

4. What are your greatest lessons learned on leadership?

When it comes to good leadership, character matters. Leadership is more about the followers than it is about the leaders, and if leaders realize that, they will be more effective.

5. Do you have any final thoughts or tips to leave with us today?

Leadership does indeed matter. But so does followership. We need to hold our leaders accountable and make sure that they are working for the common good and not for themselves. We all play a part in leadership, whether it is simply by voting or by taking “grassroots” action to make changes and accomplish shared goals.

Some of us will naturally “step up” to lead; others will be recruited. In any case, it’s important to work on leadership. It’s not something that comes naturally to people, so development is essential, and even the very best leaders realize that they need to continue working to get better.

item.title: What Makes Jerks Tick Like Time Bombs
item.description:
Motivation

What Makes Jerks Tick Like Time Bombs

Personal Perpsective: From the origins of life to our current jerk epidemic.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • People call each other jerks without wondering what they mean by it.
  • Psychologists have had trouble pinning down personality disorders.
  • Even psychologists use intuitive "skyhooked" terms to describe behavior without explaining it.
  • Explaining motivations in strictly physical terms would impose useful rigor on our diagnostic practices.

I called my book on jerks "advanced psychoproctology for beginners," and defined beginners as people who know a jerk when they see one but have never stopped to wonder what distinguishes a jerk. My own psychoproctology research was inspired by that question: What is a butthead since it can’t just be anyone I happen to butt heads with?

Collaboration with Terrence Deacon and the Evolution of Language

I’ve done this research while collaborating closely for 30 years with Terrence Deacon, a Harvard/Berkeley biologist who studies how humans evolved language, and how it transforms us from just another mid-sized mammal into the radically different creatures we are.

All organisms interpret, respond, and communicate. But language is different. Humans are born parasitic on our local culture’s maintenance of what people who study such things call “symbols”. Symbols are social conventions – letters, numbers, words, etc. – that are not inherently connected with what they represent.

Take the word “dog”. It doesn’t resemble or point to a dog. It’s not a picture of a dog, which would make it “iconic.” It’s not the sound of a dog barking in the next room, which would make it “indexical” – indicating or pointing to a nearby dog. The word “dog” is a symbol, some squiggles on a screen or sounds in the air, that, as toddlers, we English-speakers learn to associate with dogs.

A photo of a dog, or the sound of a dog barking, has inherent reference. The squiggles or sound “dog” don’t. They’re what we call “tokens,” physical forms with no inherent meaning. Humans assign meaning to them by social convention. Only humans do that to any extent. All other organisms get by with icons and indexes, in other words, resemblances and pointers.

AI’s Relationship to Tokens and Symbols

AI doesn’t even do that. We input human-generated tokens into AI. AI processes the tokens. It doesn’t interpret them. AI is not a symbol interpreter; it’s a token processor. We feed it tokens that we interpret as symbols; it outputs tokens that we interpret as symbols.

Humans are the earth’s only fully symbolic species. With tokens we interpret as symbols, we can imagine anything present or absent, real or unreal. We can make up words for anything and then combine these words to conceive of anything: A rainbow-colored rhino in a pink tutu twirling the universe on its horn, a God who likes us best, a cure for cancer, all manner of amazing contraptions. Symbols make us the radically imaginative, creative, visionary, and delusional species we are.

The Dark Side of Symbolic Imagination: Human Delusion

Also, the anxious and obnoxious creatures we can be. Most organisms are parasites or predators, but only humans can become total jerks or would be tempted to. Being a jerk is an exclusively human thing, made possible by our ability to play god, imagining anything, including that we are gods, uplifted, as if by an imaginary skyhook, into some supreme imaginary realm.

article continues after advertisement

Alas, we are not gods. We’re stuck in the real physical world.

In my work with Deacon, I distinguish between skyhooked and grounded words. Skyhooked words are intuitive. They come naturally to us once we’ve mastered a language. They’re practical. We use them all day with unconscious fluency. They’re habit-words, like the way people call each other jerks without ever wondering what they mean by it.

In the sciences we try to be more rigorous than that. We make sure our words are consistent with one another, and we test whether they fit the real world. And yet they’re still skyhooked, suspended above the physical world despite science’s rigorous description and observation.

Occasionally, there’s a breakthrough that imposes greater rigor on scientific words. We used to assume that heat was an immaterial substance called “caloric” that moved from place to place. Once we figured out the physics of it, we realized heat is the equalization of molecular speed, in other words, the second law of thermodynamics.

In the 1700’s, Linnaeus, the founding father of careful creature-naming, built a family tree of life based on similarity, resemblance, or, in a word, iconicity. In the 1950s, biologists began to refine Linnaeus’ tree of life based on common ancestry, as inferred from DNA.

Psychology has had a harder time imposing rigor on its technical terms. It’s where we get the reputation for psychobabble. It’s not just prejudice against psychology. It’s a real problem. Allan Horwitz’s history of personality disorder diagnosis exposes the hard time we’re having pinning down what’s what. The field can be a bit like a tower of psychobabble.

I’ll argue that that’s because psychology is not yet grounded. It relies on skyhooked words.

For example, psychology studies motivation, but we still lack a grounded physical account of what it is. We know it happens in bodies and involves matter. But the matter is not itself motivated. Biochemicals don’t have motivations.

Lacking a physical explanation for motivation, psychology just assumes that when we see physical effort, we can infer motivation. Motivation is a bit like caloric, an imaginable mojo. It’s a bit like “soul” or “spirit,” an unexplained explanation. Psychologists make family trees of related motivations. We test and refine these models. But they’re still skyhooked.

Deacon does something different, which I call "grounded naming." You start with the most fundamental properties in physical chemistry. You ground all naming in it. No skyhooks allowed. In our thirty years of collaboration with other researchers, we’ve been building a family tree of motivations, developed exclusively within physics – no assumed or unexplained concepts.

article continues after advertisement

For us, the grounding in physics is super simple: Two basic and universal physical concepts:

  1. Nature is all matter/form: All matter has form, shape, or dimension. You could call form pres-absences, relative presences and absences of matter, for example the way you’re unlikely to find matter in the middle of a donut. And all form occurs in matter. In other words, there’s no formless matter or immaterial form. The back story on this is interesting. Plato was devoted to skyhook naming. He assumed that there were ideal immaterial forms in some mystical realm. His student Aristotle disagreed. There’s not a second realm of immaterial forms. There’s just the obvious: Form happens in matter, and matter always has form or another.

2. Matter is conserved. Form is not. Form gets deformed over time. Cars rust, houses collapse, living beings die. The matter still exists, but the form is gone. That’s called the second law of thermodynamics, but it’s really the first law of everything.

Starting with just those two concepts, we have to explain the emergence of motivation. And from those two, we get a hint at how to do it:

There are durable objects made of matter that is tightly bound together. Their forms degenerate slowly. Living beings are almost the opposite. We don’t conserve matter, but we do conserve form.

How Living Beings Regenerate Form as a Fundamental Motivation

Think about it. We’re not made of matter; we’re made through matter, the matter passing through us. We regenerate our form with that matter (and energy, but I’m simplifying here). Regenerating our form is life’s most fundamental motivation. It’s the struggle for existence – a living being’s struggle to regenerate its form faster than it degenerates.

Alas, we are falling apart. Nothing escapes the first law of everything. But we’re giving it a run for its money. We run to stay in place. We run to outpace our own form-degeneration. And we pass on our form to offspring.

item.title: A Trick That Can Help Reduce Our Frustration and Suffering
item.description:
Attention

A Trick That Can Help Reduce Our Frustration and Suffering

Paying attention to this one word can shift your emotions.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • The word "should" is ingrained in our brain as a source of learning and growth.
  • But the expetation-reality gap can become the source of our suffering and disappointment.
  • Pausing when we use the word "should" and examining our expectations may help shift our narratives.
  • We have control over our beliefs, decisions, and character even when reality does not go our way.

My patient Henry

Imagine you are 53, working a job that you mastered, paying bills, and enjoying your family life. One day, you start to notice a tremor in your hands. You are stiffer and slower to walk. You attribute this to middle age but mention this to your primary care physician. The next thing you know, you are sitting in a neurologist’s office and are diagnosed with Parkinson’s Disease.

Henry (his name has been changed) suffered this fate, but what tortured him most over the course of the next few years were not the symptoms of Parkinson’s.

"I should be working. I am still young. I should not have to go on disability.”

Losing his identity as a provider for the family was the biggest blow. He started to suffer from depression and anxiety.

A few months ago, Henry strained his back, which led to multiple emergency room visits and a setback for his mental health.

In a follow-up clinic visit, Henry’s wife, who always accompanied him to his visits and was supportive throughout the years, seemed to have lost her wits.

“You should be taking your medicine on time, and you should have been exercising like the doctor said.”

She was merely repeating the same advice I had been giving him for years.

Yet when I heard it coming from her, something suddenly felt wrong.

The advice hadn't changed.

So why did it suddenly sound cruel?

The one word that torments us

I realized I was using the exact same word “should” that had been tormenting Henry.

The word “should” is uttered every day, both to ourselves and to others.

“I should be able to do basic things like play with my grandson. Why am I so tired?”

Another of my patients with Parkinson’s said this on the exact same day.

We all have goals. Aspiring to the idealized self, our goal, is the essence of human growth.

Sometimes, the word “should” helps us orient and move one step closer to that goal.

Neuroscience tells us that the concept of “should” is deeply ingrained in our brains. Our brains constantly compare reality with expectation. Every mismatch generates an error signal that pushes us to learn, adapt, and improve.

Without this mechanism, we would never acquire new skills or solve problems.

But the same system that allows us to grow can also become a source of suffering when every difference between reality and expectation becomes a personal failure.

Reality-expectation gap is ingrained to our brains.
Source: Michiko Bruno/AI generated

More than 2,500 years ago, Buddhism recognized that suffering arises from this gap. The First Noble Truth describes dukkha—this is often translated as “life is full of suffering” but could be better understood as a persistent sense that life never quite matches our expectations.

Interestingly, the Stoic philosophers arrived at a remarkably similar conclusion from the opposite side of the world and proposed to focus on what we have control over (our beliefs, decisions, and character) and let go of things we have no control over (our body, property, reputation, and other people’s behavior).

Making the linguistic shift

So here is some practical advice.

We can reduce our frustration and suffering by starting to pay attention to our vocabulary.

If you catch yourself using the word “should," pause.

Ask yourself, Who am I saying this to? Why am I using this word? What assumption am I making? Can I reframe it – and rephrase it?

Rather than saying, "I should exercise," try, "I'd like to try to exercise today."

Rather than "I should be grateful," it is okay to accept and say, "I'm disappointed today."

Small linguistic shifts can result in emotional shifts.

This does not mean we can remove all disappointments. Pain and disappointment will be ubiquitous in our lives. In a way, that is one constant of life. It is integral because of how we and our brains evolved to be who we are now.

But the judgment we make towards ourselves creates additional, unnecessary suffering on top of the pain and suffering that is inherent.

***

My last visit with Henry caught me by surprise. He came in with a big smile. Always eloquent, his wife spoke first.

“We came up with a way for him to take medicine one time. He is doing the exercise when he can, and we just came back from a trip to Texas last month; our kids also said he is doing much better compared to last year.”

Not to be outdone, Henry opened his mouth.

“Our youngest had a daughter. We love our granddaughter, and I want to live for her.”

He was finally able to feel better, not because his Parkinson’s improved, but because he was able to create his own meaning in life.

And that is something we have control over, even if our day is not going our way.
